lead: This unit is about code that runs on the server: PHP scripts that build pages, Java servlets and JSP that run in a container, and a Spring Boot REST service that stores data through JPA. After it you can set up a PHP or Tomcat server, read form data safely, keep a login state with cookies or sessions, and expose a small JSON API backed by a database.
about: The unit moves from a single PHP file to a deployed Java service. Chapter 4.1 fixes PHP syntax, variables, types and operators; 4.2 puts that code on Apache through XAMPP and compares Tomcat and IIS. Chapter 4.3 adds decisions, loops, functions and arrays, which 4.4 uses for string processing and regular expressions. Chapter 4.5 reads GET and POST form data, and 4.6 keeps state across requests with cookies and sessions. Chapter 4.7 moves the same request-response idea to Java servlets and their life cycle. Chapter 4.8, which only a few universities teach, shows how JSP becomes a servlet and how JSF adds components. Chapter 4.9, also advanced, builds a Spring Boot REST API with JPA.

chapters.idea: PHP is a server-side language: a .php file mixes HTML with <?php ... ?> blocks, and variables are $ names filled at run time.
chapters.depth: PHP Hypertext Preprocessor; a request reaches Apache, PHP parses and runs the file, and HTML goes back. Syntax: tags, comments, echo and print, semicolon at the end of a statement. Variables: $name, no type declaration, case-sensitive names, type juggling; constants with define() and const. Data types: bool, int, float, string, array, object, resource and NULL; is_* checks and casting. Operators: arithmetic, assignment, comparison (== and ===), logical, string concatenation with ., increment, ternary, null coalescing ?? and spaceship <=>; operator precedence.

figure.title: Pay calculation
figure.aria: A flow from price 250 and quantity 3 to total 750, GST 135, payable 885 and the printed line.
figure.caption: The shaded total and GST feed the payable amount; the last box is the output.

chapters.example: Question: a shop script sets $price = 250 rupees and $qty = 3. It computes $total = $price * $qty, adds 18% GST, and prints the payable amount. Give the PHP and the output. Answer: $total is 750; GST is 750 * 0.18 = 135; payable is 750 + 135 = 885. The output is Pay: ₹885.
chapters.trap: Using + to join strings, or == where === is needed; $price and price are different names, and a string '250' behaves as a number only in arithmetic.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: HTTP request and client-server; Unit 2: basic HTML.
chapters.leave: Control flow and arrays to 4.3; form input to 4.5; file and directory functions are outside these nine chapters.

chapters.idea: A PHP file needs a web server with a PHP interpreter, while a servlet needs a servlet container; XAMPP packages Apache, PHP and MySQL for a laptop.
chapters.depth: XAMPP: Apache, MySQL/MariaDB, PHP and Perl; control panel; htdocs document root; php.ini and httpd.conf. Apache: ports 80 and 443, modules, virtual hosts; PHP as a module or through FastCGI. Tomcat: servlet and JSP container, default port 8080, webapps folder, server.xml, WAR deployment. IIS: Windows web server, port 80, FastCGI for PHP. localhost, hosts file and port conflicts. Some syllabi call this environment setup or installation and version information.

figure.title: Three server paths
figure.aria: A browser connects to Apache, Tomcat and IIS; Apache runs PHP with MySQL, Tomcat runs servlets, and IIS runs PHP through FastCGI.
figure.caption: A browser reaches three server types; PHP runs in Apache or through IIS FastCGI, and servlets run in Tomcat.

chapters.example: Question: a Windows laptop runs XAMPP at C:/xampp. The file C:/xampp/htdocs/shop/pay.php must be opened in a browser, and a shop.war is deployed to Tomcat. Give the two URLs and their ports. Port 80 is already used by another program: what do you change? Answer: PHP URL http://localhost/shop/pay.php uses port 80; servlet URL http://localhost:8080/shop/ uses 8080. Free port 80, or change Apache's Listen 80 in httpd.conf; if you choose 8080, move Tomcat's connector to another port in server.xml.
chapters.trap: Calling Tomcat a PHP server, or putting PHP files in Tomcat's webapps folder; XAMPP serves PHP from htdocs.
chapters.leave: PHP language details to 4.1 and 4.3; servlet code to 4.7; Docker and CI/CD deployment to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Control statements choose and repeat work, functions wrap reusable work with their own scope, and PHP arrays are ordered maps that a foreach can walk.
chapters.depth: if, elseif and else; switch and match; while, do-while, for and foreach; break and continue. Functions: parameters, default values, return, variable scope, global and static. Recursion: base case and recursive call; factorial and Fibonacci. Arrays: indexed, associative and multidimensional; count, sort, array_push, array_keys, in_array; foreach by value and by key. Some syllabi call this decision making and loop controls.

figure.aria: A recursion chain for fact(4): fact(4) calls fact(3), then fact(2), fact(1), and stops at 1.
figure.caption: fact(4) unwinds to 24; the base case fact(1)=1 stops the recursion.

chapters.example: Question: write a recursive PHP function fact($n) and use a for loop to print the factorials of 1 to 5. Trace fact(4). Answer: output is 1, 2, 6, 24, 120. The call goes fact(4) = 4 * fact(3) = 4 * 6 = 24; fact(3) = 3 * fact(2) = 3 * 2 = 6; fact(2) = 2 * 1 = 2; base case fact(1) = 1.
chapters.trap: A recursive function without a base case; also forgetting that a function cannot see an outside variable unless it is passed in or declared global.
chapters.leave: String functions to 4.4; form arrays such as $_POST to 4.5; database loops to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: PHP strings are manipulated with built-in functions, and regular expressions match patterns through PCRE functions such as preg_match and preg_replace.
chapters.depth: strlen, strpos, substr, str_replace, strtolower, strtoupper, ucfirst, trim, explode, implode, sprintf, htmlspecialchars and nl2br. PCRE: delimiters /.../, anchors ^ and $, character classes such as [6-9], digit, word and space classes, quantifiers * + ? and {9}, groups, alternation, modifiers i, m and u. preg_match returns 1 or 0; preg_match_all, preg_replace and preg_split. Validation of phone, email and date; escaping output; regular expressions are for patterns, not full HTML parsing.

figure.title: Phone check
figure.aria: The input with a space is cleaned to ten digits, then matched against an anchored pattern; result 1 is valid and 0 is invalid.
figure.caption: Spaces are removed first; the anchored pattern accepts a 10-digit number starting 6–9.

chapters.example: Question: a form sends $phone = '98765 43210'. Remove spaces with preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone), then test preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $phone). Show the cleaned value and the result for this input and for '5876543210'. Answer: cleaned value is 9876543210; the regex returns 1, so it is valid. The second number returns 0 because it starts with 5, not 6–9.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the delimiters, or using ^ and $ without checking the whole string; a backslash in a double-quoted PHP string may need escaping, so single quotes are safer.
chapters.leave: Form handling to 4.5; Unicode and mb_* details can be looked up when needed.

chapters.idea: A form sends its fields as name=value pairs: GET puts them in the URL, POST puts them in the request body, and PHP reads them from $_GET or $_POST.
chapters.depth: form action and method, name attributes, submit. Query string encoding; GET length limits, bookmarkable and idempotent; POST for passwords and changes. $_GET, $_POST and $_REQUEST; isset, empty and filter_input; validation and output escaping; $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']; self-submit; redirect after POST. File uploads need enctype multipart/form-data, but their storage details are left out here.

figure.aria: Two request-response pairs: a GET with name and marks in the URL, then a POST with the same fields in the body.
figure.caption: GET puts name and marks in the URL; POST puts the same fields in the request body.

chapters.example: Question: a form sends name=Anu and marks=78 to result.php. Give the GET URL and the POST request body, and PHP that prints Anu scored 78 after checking marks is 0–100. Answer: GET is result.php?name=Anu&marks=78. POST body is name=Anu&marks=78 under POST /result.php. PHP reads $_POST['name'] and (int) $_POST['marks'], rejects marks outside 0–100, and prints htmlspecialchars($name) . ' scored ' . $marks.
chapters.trap: Trusting $_REQUEST or raw input; printing user input without htmlspecialchars opens XSS; GET leaks a password into the URL and browser history.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 HTML forms; Unit 1 HTTP methods; 4.3 arrays.
chapters.leave: Cookies and sessions to 4.6; file upload storage and directory functions are outside these nine chapters; SQL insertion to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: HTTP forgets each request, so cookies store small values on the browser and sessions store larger values on the server under a session ID.
chapters.depth: Cookie: setcookie(name, value, expires, path, domain, secure, httponly, samesite); $_COOKIE; deletion by a past expiry; small size limit; no output before the header. Session: session_start, $_SESSION, session_id, session_regenerate_id, session_destroy and garbage collection; session cookie PHPSESSID; security with httponly, secure and samesite; session fixation; never store a password in a cookie. Some syllabi call this session tracking or state management.

figure.aria: A login creates session abc123 on the server; the browser stores the session ID and sends it back when asking for the cart.
figure.caption: The browser holds only the session ID; user Anu and the ₹750 cart stay in the server-side store.

chapters.example: Question: Anu logs in. PHP creates session ID abc123 and stores user = Anu and cart_total = 750 rupees. Show the Set-Cookie header for a 30-minute cookie, the next request, and the PHP that sets it. What happens after 30 idle minutes? Answer: Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=abc123; Max-Age=1800; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax. The next request sends Cookie: PHPSESSID=abc123. Code: session_set_cookie_params(['lifetime'=>1800,'httponly'=>true,'samesite'=>'Lax']); session_start(); $_SESSION['user']='Anu'; $_SESSION['cart_total']=750;. After 30 idle minutes the browser drops the cookie; the next visit starts a new session, and old server data is removed by garbage collection, not instantly.
chapters.trap: Calling session_start after any output causes headers already sent; a cookie is not encrypted, so never put a password or secret in it.
chapters.leave: Servlet sessions to 4.7; JWT and token security to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A servlet is one Java object managed by a container: init runs once, service runs for every request, and destroy runs once at shutdown.
chapters.depth: Servlet API; HttpServlet; doGet and doPost; @WebServlet or web.xml; ServletRequest and ServletResponse; parameters, headers, content type and writer; life cycle; one instance and many threads, so avoid mutable instance fields; forward versus sendRedirect; init-params and context-params; HttpSession, linked to 4.6. Container such as Tomcat. Older code imports javax.servlet; newer code imports jakarta.servlet.

figure.title: Servlet life cycle
figure.aria: A servlet is loaded, initialized once, services each request through doGet or doPost, and is destroyed once at shutdown.
figure.caption: One servlet object: init runs once, service runs for every request, destroy runs at shutdown.

chapters.example: Question: GreetServlet is mapped to /greet and reads name=Anu and marks=78. Give doGet and trace the life cycle for three requests. Answer: protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res) throws IOException { String name = req.getParameter("name"); int marks = Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("marks")); res.setContentType("text/html"); PrintWriter out = res.getWriter(); out.println(name + " scored " + marks); }. Output is Anu scored 78. The container calls init() once, service() three times, and destroy() once at shutdown.
chapters.trap: Putting per-user data in an instance field of the servlet; all requests share that one object. Also doPost will not run for a GET.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 Tomcat; Unit 1 application server; Java classes.
chapters.leave: JSP and JSF to 4.8; Spring Boot to 4.9; session cookie details back to 4.6.

chapters.idea: JSP turns an HTML page with Java into a servlet, and JSF builds on servlets with reusable UI components and managed beans.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. JSP life cycle: translation, compilation, init, service and destroy; directives page, include and taglib; scriptlet, expression and declaration; implicit objects request, response, session, application and out; EL ${param.name}; JSTL core tags; MVC. JSF: Facelets .xhtml, managed beans, h:form, h:inputText, h:commandButton, validation, navigation and the component tree.

figure.title: JSP translation
figure.aria: hello.jsp is translated to Java source, compiled to a class, loaded as a servlet, and services an HTML response.
figure.caption: A JSP is translated and compiled into a servlet once, then service writes HTML.

chapters.example: Question: a JSP page must show Anu scored 78 from URL parameters name=Anu and marks=78. Write the JSP with EL. Then show the JSF input fields and button that bind the same values to a bean. Answer: JSP body is ${param.name} scored ${param.marks}. A JSF Facelet has an h:form with two h:inputText fields bound to #{marksBean.name} and #{marksBean.marks}, and an h:commandButton with action result; result.xhtml reads #{marksBean.name} and #{marksBean.marks}.
chapters.trap: JSP is not JavaScript; scriptlets run on the server. A JSP becomes a servlet, so HTML output must still be escaped when it comes from users.
chapters.leave: Full JSF component libraries and Spring MVC to 4.9; front-end frameworks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Spring Boot starts an embedded server, @RestController turns methods into JSON endpoints, and Spring Data JPA turns repository calls into SQL.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Start from a Spring Boot project; starters for web and data-jpa; application.properties for the datasource; @SpringBootApplication; @RestController, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PathVariable, @RequestBody and ResponseEntity; embedded Tomcat; runnable JAR. JPA: @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, repository extends JpaRepository; findById, findAll and save; H2 or MySQL. JSON request and response; validation; optional service layer. Actuator, Docker and CI/CD are outside this chapter.

figure.aria: A GET for student 1 goes from controller to repository, becomes a SQL select, and returns JSON with Anu and 78.
figure.caption: Spring MVC sends the request to a controller; Spring Data JPA turns findById into SQL.

chapters.example: Question: a student table has id, name and marks. Expose GET /api/students/1 for id 1, name Anu, marks 78. Give the entity, repository, controller and JSON. Then POST Ravi with marks 65 and give the response. Answer: JSON is {"id":1,"name":"Anu","marks":78}. The POST body {"name":"Ravi","marks":65} returns 201 with {"id":2,"name":"Ravi","marks":65}. Entity: @Entity class Student with @Id @GeneratedValue Long id, String name, int marks and a no-arg constructor. Repository: interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository for entity Student and ID Long. Controller: @RestController with @GetMapping for /api/students/{id}; the method calls repo.findById(id).orElseThrow().
chapters.trap: An @Entity needs a no-arg constructor and an @Id; a JpaRepository is an interface, not a class. Returning entities directly can leak fields or trigger lazy loading, so a DTO is safer.
chapters.prereq: 4.7 servlet request-response; Unit 6 REST, JSON and databases.
chapters.leave: Spring Security and JWT to Unit 6; Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD and Actuator monitoring are outside this chapter.
